summary: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheezing, cough, chest tightness and breathlessness. Symptoms come and go and are often triggered by dust, smoke, pollution, cold air, infections or exercise. It can be controlled with proper medical care.
symptoms: Cough, often worse at night or early morning
Symptoms triggered by dust, smoke, cold air, exercise or infections
causes: Airway inflammation influenced by genetics and allergies
Triggers include dust mites, pollen, smoke, air pollution, strong smells, cold air, respiratory infections and exercise
risk_factors: Family history of asthma or allergies
Tobacco smoke exposure and indoor smoke (for example cooking fuel)

tests.name: Spirometry (lung function test)
tests.purpose: Measures airflow and how it improves after an inhaler.

preparation.other: The lab may ask you to avoid smoking, heavy exercise or a large meal beforehand, and may give instructions about when to take or hold your usual inhalers.

tests.exceptions: Do not stop any prescribed medicine on your own; follow the doctor's or lab's instruction. Young children may not be able to perform spirometry.

preparation.other: Technique is taught by the doctor or nurse.

tests.name: Chest X-ray, allergy tests or blood tests
tests.purpose: Used to look for other causes or triggers.

prevention: Reduce dust exposure at home; use clean cooking fuel and good ventilation
On high-pollution days, limit strenuous outdoor activity as advised by your doctor
lifestyle: Keep a written asthma action plan from your doctor
Take preventer and reliever inhalers only as prescribed and learn the correct technique
Get the doctor's advice on vaccines such as the flu vaccine
red_flags: Severe breathlessness or unable to speak in full sentences
Blue or grey lips or face
Reliever inhaler not helping or needed again and again
when_to_consult: Wheeze, night cough or breathlessness that keeps returning
Increasing need for the reliever inhaler
special_populations: Children: recurrent cough or wheeze should be assessed by a paediatrician
Pregnancy: do not stop asthma medicine without medical advice; uncontrolled asthma is also risky
Older adults: asthma can overlap with COPD and heart disease; the doctor will assess

faqs.a: It is usually a long-term condition that can be well controlled with the right treatment and trigger control.

faqs.q: Do I stop my inhaler before a lung test?
faqs.a: Only if your doctor or lab tells you to. Do not stop on your own.
